title: Design a small chat app
summary: Plan saved messages and live delivery for a small chat. Handle repeated sends, missing connections, message order, and private group access.
introduction: A spoken message can be lost when someone walks out of the room. A chat app should keep messages so a person can catch up after reconnecting. Fast live delivery is useful, but saved history is the foundation.
learningObjectives: Separate saving a message from delivering or reading it
Use stable message IDs and per-conversation order

blocks.text: Plan text chat for 100 school club members in small groups. Members send messages, view group history, and catch up after a short disconnection. Video calls, huge public rooms, and typing indicators are outside the first version.

A **WebSocket** is a connection that lets a browser and service send updates to each other without opening a new request for every update. It helps with live delivery, but does not save history by itself.

blocks.alt: A sender uses a message ID. The chat service checks access and saves the message. It delivers now or after reconnecting, then records confirmation.
blocks.caption: A saved message is not the same as a delivered or read message. IDs help the receiver hide duplicates after a retry.

blocks.code:
Small group-chat design
Conversation: conversationId, name
Member: conversationId, readerId
Message: messageId, conversationId, senderId, clientMessageId, sequence, text

Send {conversationId, clientMessageId, text}
1. Check the sender's identity and current membership.
2. Save the message once for this sender/clientMessageId in the conversation.
3. Assign its next sequence number within the conversation.
4. Save a delivery-event record with the message, then commit.
5. Tell the sender the message is saved.
6. Send live updates to connected permitted members.

Reconnect {conversationId, afterSequence}
Check membership, then return saved messages after that sequence in order.
Receivers ignore repeated messageIds.
blocks.title: Worked design plan
blocks.caption: Read this as a design plan. It is not a running server or an API you can call.

blocks.text: Give each saved message a stable place

The browser creates a client message ID before sending. It reuses that ID when retrying the same message. The service saves a uniqueness rule for the sender, conversation, and client ID, and rejects reuse with different message text.

A **sequence number** gives each saved message a position in one conversation: 1, 2, 3, and so on. Assign it safely with the save. This plan promises order within a conversation, not one global order for every chat.
Follow a message and a reconnection

items: A member sends message m7. The service checks group membership and text length, then saves the message and a delivery-event record together.
The service replies "saved". This does not mean every recipient received or read the message.
A worker sends updates over active connections. It may send an update again after a retry, so receivers remove repeats by message ID.
A disconnected member returns with their last seen sequence, such as 12. The service checks membership again and returns later saved messages in order.
The browser merges history and live updates by message ID and sequence. If there is a gap, it asks for missing history rather than guessing.

blocks.text: Saving a delivery-event record with the message prevents a crash between saving and announcing it from silently losing the announcement. A worker can retry later. History is still available while live delivery is delayed.
Plan the boundaries and the load

Use a normal history request for catch-up and a WebSocket for live updates. Both must check access. When someone leaves a private group, stop future live delivery and apply the current history-access rule.

Start with one chat service, a database, and a worker. Index history by conversation and sequence. If traffic grows, active connections may be spread across servers with a shared message-routing layer. That extra layer should follow measured need.

A very large room makes each message fan out to many recipients. **Fan-out** means one event creating many deliveries. Bound each connection's waiting queue; a slow connection can reconnect and fetch saved history instead of using endless memory.

items: A sender sees no reply after sending m7 and sends it again with the same client message ID. What should history contain?
One saved message. The service returns the saved outcome for that ID. If the sender used a fresh ID, the service might correctly treat it as a new message.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not label a saved message as "read" just because it was stored or sent over a connection. Saved, delivered, and read are different events.
